topic: NVIDIA-Certified Professional: Accelerated Data Science (NCP-ADS) exam preparation - professional-level GPU-accelerated data science using the RAPIDS suite (cuDF, cuML, cuGraph), Dask, DALI, and CUDA to build, scale, and optimize end-to-end data science workflows on NVIDIA GPUs
exam_format: Approximately 60-70 multiple-choice questions, 120 minutes, taken online with remote proctoring. NVIDIA does NOT publish an official passing score or official per-domain percentage weightings for NCP-ADS, so the domain weights in this course are editorial estimates that reflect the emphasis of NVIDIA's published exam topic list, not NVIDIA's official figures. The certification is valid for two years. Exam fee is approximately USD 200 and varies by region; present any fee as approximate and advise candidates to confirm current NVIDIA pricing.
question_types: multiple choice (single answer and multiple response) and scenario-based questions about designing, scaling, and optimizing GPU-accelerated data science pipelines with the RAPIDS ecosystem
audience: Data scientists, ML engineers, and data engineers who already work with pandas/scikit-learn and want to scale to GPU-accelerated data science with RAPIDS on NVIDIA GPUs. Comfortable with Python, Jupyter, SQL, and core data-science concepts; some GPU familiarity helps. The professional-level companion to the NVIDIA NCA-ADS (Accelerated Data Science Associate) course already in this catalog.
author: Aseem Mankotia

domains.name: GPU-Accelerated Data Science Fundamentals
domains.notes: Why and how GPUs accelerate data science: GPU vs CPU architecture, CUDA and the CUDA-X data science stack, the RAPIDS ecosystem (cuDF, cuML, cuGraph, cuSpatial), memory model and host-to-device transfer costs, and when GPU acceleration does (and does not) pay off. Setting up RAPIDS environments (conda, containers, NGC). Choosing GPU vs CPU execution for a described dataset size and workflow.

domains.name: Data Preparation and Manipulation with cuDF
domains.notes: The largest domain (editorial estimate): cleaning, transforming, joining, grouping, and standardizing tabular data with cuDF as a near-drop-in GPU replacement for pandas; handling strings, datetimes, nulls, and categoricals on the GPU; the cuDF-to-pandas bridge and interoperability; generating synthetic data with RAPIDS; and managing data pipelines for performance and memory efficiency. Choosing the correct cuDF pattern (and when to fall back to pandas) for a described transformation.

domains.name: ETL and Distributed Processing
domains.notes: Scaling beyond a single GPU: ETL design with GPU acceleration, distributed and multi-GPU processing with Dask and dask-cuDF, partitioning and data caching strategies, out-of-core workflows for datasets larger than GPU memory, and choosing the right library and cluster topology for data manipulation at scale. Reading/writing Parquet/ORC efficiently. Selecting single-GPU vs multi-GPU vs multi-node for a described throughput and data-volume requirement.

domains.name: Advanced Analytics
domains.notes: GPU-accelerated analytics beyond basic ETL: exploratory data analysis at scale, time-series analysis and anomaly detection, graph analytics with cuGraph (PageRank, centrality, community detection), and geospatial analysis with cuSpatial at an awareness level. Feature engineering for large tabular datasets. Choosing the correct analytics approach and library for a described problem (e.g., fraud graph vs time-series anomaly).

domains.name: Model Training and Acceleration
domains.notes: GPU-accelerated machine learning: cuML for regression, classification, and clustering at GPU speed; GPU-accelerated XGBoost; rapid hyperparameter tuning; and feeding data-loading pipelines into deep learning with DALI and PyTorch/TensorFlow. Matching cuML/XGBoost algorithms to a described modeling task and dataset scale, and understanding where the data-science pipeline hands off to model training.

domains.name: Best Practices, Profiling, and Optimization
domains.notes: Getting the most out of the GPU: memory-efficient techniques, batching, mixed precision, avoiding unnecessary host-device transfers, and profiling with tools such as DLProf and Nsight to find bottlenecks. Reproducibility, environment management, and production best practices for accelerated pipelines. Choosing the correct optimization or profiling action for a described performance bottleneck.

extra_guidance: NVIDIA-Certified Professional: Accelerated Data Science (NCP-ADS) is the professional-level companion to the NVIDIA NCA-ADS (Associate) course already in this catalog - it goes deeper into scaling and optimizing GPU-accelerated data science with the full RAPIDS ecosystem. CRITICAL accuracy note: NVIDIA does NOT publish official per-domain percentage weightings or a fixed passing score for NCP-ADS, so present the domain NAMES from NVIDIA's published exam topics but mark the weights as editorial estimates (leading '~'), never as NVIDIA's official figures - state this where weights appear. This is a scenario and tool-selection exam: the real skill is choosing the RIGHT RAPIDS library, execution mode (single-GPU vs Dask multi-GPU vs out-of-core), and optimization for a described data-science requirement, so practice questions MUST be scenario-based ('MOST efficient / BEST scaling / correct library') and MUST use exact tool and API names (cuDF, cuML, cuGraph, cuSpatial, dask-cuDF, DALI, CUDA, XGBoost, DLProf, Nsight, NGC). Cover the recurring decision pairs relentlessly: pandas vs cuDF; single-GPU vs dask-cuDF multi-GPU; cuML vs scikit-learn; GPU XGBoost vs CPU; in-memory vs out-of-core; where the GPU transfer cost outweighs the speedup. Anchor everything to real RAPIDS behavior; do NOT invent APIs or limits. Labs are read-and-understand RAPIDS walkthroughs (accelerate a pandas pipeline with cuDF, scale it with dask-cuDF, train cuML/XGBoost models, run a cuGraph analysis, profile with DLProf/Nsight), not deep hands-on GPU coding. Frame the credential honestly as 'exam-focused preparation' - never promise a pass or use the word 'guarantee' in any form (Udemy compliance). Final chapter must be a full exam simulation with a time-management strategy for the ~60-70 question, 120-minute format. Present the exam fee as approximate (~USD 200) and note the certification is valid two years; advise verifying current NVIDIA pricing. Scan the practice bank for stray other-vendor terms (AWS/Azure/GCP) before upload per the pipeline compliance rules.
